Reproducing ten Brinke et al. (2017) from CRCNS cb-1¶

Paper. ten Brinke MM, Heiney SA, Wang X, Proietti-Onori M, Boele HJ, Bakermans J, Medina JF, Gao Z, De Zeeuw CI (2017). Dynamic modulation of activity in cerebellar nuclei neurons during pavlovian eyeblink conditioning in mice. eLife 6:e28132. doi:10.7554/eLife.28132. The claims file (claims/brinke-2017.yaml) was written from the version of record (PMC5760204) with its figure legends, Methods and Supplementary file 1; this attempt read the same text.

Data set. CRCNS cb-1, "Eyelid behavior and spike activity of cerebellar interpositus nucleus neurons during eyeblink conditioning in awake behaving mice", doi:10.6080/K0B85697, read anonymously from the public S3 bucket crcnsarchive under cb-1/live/. CRCNS does not version its data sets and the paper cites the data set's DOI without a version, so the version is recorded as unversioned: the files as published under cb-1/live/ (last modified 2026-02-11 in the bucket; the description is version 0.6 of 13 Dec 2017). There is no other version to choose. The one data file is eLife_dataset.mat, MD5 511cf0f257240365977d2c5960766f5d in the data set's checksums.md5; the notebook streams it into memory and checks the MD5 (the description PDF is fa19108c9385b7e66d6df95e68a30c99 and the example script eLife_dataset.m dce22a5c204e00f10b692f1b07a3eae0). A later change to the file would show as a mismatch in the first cell.

What the data set holds. 372 recordings of interpositus nucleus neurons: 270 of the first dataset (recorded over training, CS-US interval 250 ms) and 102 of the second (after training, 212 ms by the description), each with per-trial eyelid traces, spike density traces, spike times, a per-trial facilitation and CR amplitude, the mouse and the training day. It holds no recording depth, no US-only trials, no optogenetic sessions and no Purkinje cell recordings.

Outside data. Recording depth is taken from the paper's Source data 1 (Additional files of doi:10.7554/eLife.28132), the file of the version of record on the eLife site (elife-28132-data1-v2.mat, MD5 3ca8f91c5371e88c12f5eb32b3b209c6, checked when it is streamed), as the claims file's opening comment names it. Only its Depth is used; the link claim source-data-1-link matches its cells to the data set's by order and checks the values both hold. Source data 1 gives no depth for the second dataset's 102 cells.

Method details taken from the paper, and readings. The helper module ipn.py says where each parameter comes from. Where the claims file names readings, every one is run; the class of a cell (facilitation, suppression, none) is run under the claims file's two baseline-correction readings, (a) and (b), and under a variant of this attempt's own, (a+), the Methods' "mean above-baseline activity within the baseline itself" averaged over the above-baseline bins only; no outcome rests on (a+) alone. Reading (b) on each cell's average trace gives the authors' per-cell facilitation in Source data 1. The second dataset's classes use the claims file's two windows, 12-212 ms (adopted) and 0-200 ms; 0-212 ms is shown as a variant where the verifier asked for it. CR amplitude at US onset is run as the data set's own crAmplitude (which this notebook finds is the eyelid 13 ms before the stated US onset) and as computed at the stated US onset. The CS pause and peak are run under the four threshold readings of the claims file, the two windows (50-125 ms in the Methods, 50-130 ms in the Results) and two places to look for the rebound (within the window, or up to 50 ms after the trough, marked "+50", this attempt's variant). The spike-eyelid cross-correlation lags use an estimator the paper does not name: the adopted one is the cross-covariance of the two mean-subtracted traces over the segment (as MATLAB's xcov, 'coeff'), and the Pearson r of the spike segment with the eyelid re-cut at each lag is shown as a variant. The Methods' trial exclusions are not applied again: Source data 1 lists exactly the deposited trials of each cell as its valid trials. The Statistics rule for correlations needs a normality test the paper does not name; Lilliefors is used, and a Spearman-only count is printed beside each trial-by-trial count. Bootstrap p-values are fractions of 500 random datasets, so 0.000 means below 1/500. Each claim's section has its own random generator with a fixed seed.

for sdv in (3, 4, 5, 6):
    vals = []
    for i in range(0, 372, 37):
        for tr in range(3):
            s = D["spikes"][i][tr]

# The data set's per-trial crAmplitude ("eyelid amplitude at US onset ... from baseline (all datapoints where
# timeIndex < 0)") against the eyelid traces, at the stated US onset and at other times.
def crmatch(off):
    out = {1: [], 2: []}
    for i in range(372):
        e = D["eyelid"][i]
        v = (e[:, t == D["us"][i] + off][:, 0] - np.nanmean(e[:, t < 0], 1)) * 100
        out[int(D["dset"][i])].append(np.max(np.abs(v - D["cramp"][i])))
    return {k: (round(float(np.median(v)), 3), round(float(np.max(v)), 3)) for k, v in out.items()}
for off in (0, -12, -13, -14):
    print(f"crAmplitude vs eyelid at US onset {off:+d} ms: per-recording max abs difference (median, max) by set", crmatch(off))
# The data set's per-trial facilitation against readings (a), (a+) and (b) of the modulation measure on single trials
def facmatch(win_of):
    out = {1: [], 2: []}
    for i in range(372):
        ds, us = int(D["dset"][i]), int(D["us"][i])
        mod = ipn.modulation(D["sdf"][i], t, ipn.baseline_window(ds), win_of(ds, us))
        out[ds].append([np.max(np.abs(mod[f"fac_{rd}"] - D["fac"][i])) for rd in ("a", "ap", "b")])
    return {k: np.round(np.median(np.array(v), 0), 3).tolist() for k, v in out.items()}
print("facilitation, median per-recording max abs difference (Hz) for readings a, a+, b;",
      "window = last 200 ms:", facmatch(lambda ds, us: (us - 200, us)))
print("   window = CS onset to US onset:", facmatch(lambda ds, us: (0, us)))

source-data-1-link¶

The cells of the paper's Source data 1 are the cells of CRCNS cb-1 in the same order, so that the recording depth Source data 1 gives can be attached to the data set's cells.

Source: Additional files, Source data 1. Data: with_inputs. A link claim (Author, step 4).

Criterion (claims file): Added by the author of attempt brinke-2017-01 (Author, step 4). Cell i of the data set is matched to cell i of Source data 1, the order both use. The matched cells are compared on what both hold, the number of trials, the per-trial eyelid closure at US onset ('CR @ US ms' against the data set's crAmplitude) and the per-trial baseline rate ('Baseline Hz' against the spike count in the pre-CS baseline), and the same comparisons are shown with the cells shifted by one as a reference. Reproduced when at least 99% of the 372 cells agree on all three and the shifted match does not; the number of cells with a depth is reported.

SD1, sd1_md5 = ipn.load_source_data1()
print("Source data 1:", ipn.SOURCE_DATA1)
print("  MD5", sd1_md5, "pinned", ipn.SOURCE_DATA1_MD5, "match", sd1_md5 == ipn.SOURCE_DATA1_MD5)
print("  variables:", len(SD1), "| cells per variable:", sorted({len(v) for v in SD1.values()}))


def base_hz(i):
    """Per-trial spike count in the cell's baseline window (ipn.baseline_window), in Hz."""
    lo, hi = ipn.baseline_window(int(df.dset[i]))
    return np.array([np.sum((s >= lo) & (s < hi)) for s in D["spikes"][i]]) / ((hi - lo) / 1000)


def link_checks(shift=0):
    """Match data set cell i to Source data 1 cell i + shift; per-cell agreement on what both hold."""
    out = []
    for i in range(len(df)):
        j = i + shift
        if not 0 <= j < len(df):
            continue
        n = D["sdf"][i].shape[0]
        same_n = len(SD1["# Valid Trials"][j]) == n
        cr = same_n and np.allclose(SD1["CR @ US ms"][j], D["cramp"][i], atol=1e-9, equal_nan=True)
        bh = same_n and np.allclose(SD1["Baseline Hz"][j], base_hz(i), atol=1e-6)
        out.append({"cell": i, "dset": int(df.dset[i]), "trials": same_n, "CR @ US = crAmplitude": cr, "Baseline Hz = spike count": bh})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


lk = link_checks()
ids = np.array([np.unique(SD1["Cell"][i]).tolist() == [i + 1] for i in range(len(df))])
print("Source data 1 'Cell' is the cell's position (1-372), constant over its trials:", int(ids.sum()), "of", len(df))
print("cells matched by order that agree (of 270 first-dataset, 102 second-dataset cells):")
print(lk.groupby("dset")[["trials", "CR @ US = crAmplitude", "Baseline Hz = spike count"]].sum().to_string())
for sh in (-1, 1):
    l2 = link_checks(sh)
    print(f"  reference, cells shifted by {sh:+d}: same trial count {int(l2.trials.sum())}, same CR @ US {int(l2['CR @ US = crAmplitude'].sum())},"
          f" same baseline Hz {int(l2['Baseline Hz = spike count'].sum())} of {len(l2)}")

Source data 1's per-cell values against this attempt's¶

The link above shows that the deposited trials of every cell are the trials Source data 1 lists, as # Valid Trials (one entry per trial) has the deposited trial count in all 372 cells. The Methods' trial exclusions (Grubbs test on baseline SDs, eye at least half open) are therefore taken as already applied, and are not applied again here. Source data 1 also holds the authors' own per-trial CR flags and per-cell modulation and US-response values. They are compared here with this attempt's measures, to show where the selections differ. None of these values is used by any claim below: the claims file takes only recording depth from Source data 1.

# Shared definitions for the claims below.
WIN2 = "12-212"  # adopted second-dataset window (description's 212 ms interval); 0-200 ms shown beside it
WINS2 = ("12-212", "0-200")  # the claims file's two second-dataset windows
READINGS = {"a": "a", "a+": "ap", "b": "b"}  # baseline-correction readings (a) and (b) of the claims file; a+ is this attempt's variant


def cls(rd, win2=WIN2, rule="larger"):
    """Class of every recording under baseline reading rd, second-dataset window win2."""
    r = READINGS[rd]
    c1 = df[f"cls_{r}_{rule}_50-250"].where(df.dset == 1)
    c2 = df[f"cls_{r}_{rule}_{win2}"].where(df.dset == 2)
    return c1.fillna(c2)


def mag(rd, kind, win2=WIN2):
    """Facilitation (kind 'fac') or suppression depth ('sup') in Hz under reading rd."""
    r = READINGS[rd]
    return df[f"{kind}_{r}_50-250"].where(df.dset == 1).fillna(df[f"{kind}_{r}_{win2}"].where(df.dset == 2))


def amp_trials(i, which):
    """Per-trial CR amplitude (%): 'data' the data set's crAmplitude (at US onset by its description),
    'us' computed here at the stated US onset, 'max' the CS-US maximum (Methods)."""
    if which == "data":
        return D["cramp"][i]
    e = ipn.eyelid_trials(D["eyelid"][i], t, int(D["us"][i]))
    return e["amp_us"] if which == "us" else e["amp_max"]


def fmt(x, n=3):
    return np.round(x, n)

firing-rate-depth¶

In the first dataset the IpN firing frequency averaged 67 +/- 27 Hz and did not vary with recording depth (r = 0.085, p = 0.16, n = 270, Pearson).

Source: Results, Characterization of cerebellar IpN neurons, paragraph 2. Data: with_inputs.

Criterion (claims file): Firing frequency is the cell's mean rate over the 500 ms baseline (reading a) or over the whole trial (reading b), the paper does not say which; depth is the recording depth, from Source data 1 (opening comment). A claim of absence judged on the paper's test, Pearson's r at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the correlation is not significant and the mean rate is within tolerance under one reading.

Depth from Source data 1 (see source-data-1-link).

Result: reproduced, under reading (a). Over the 500 ms baseline the 270 first-dataset cells fire at 68.3 +/- 26.4 Hz, within 67 +/- 6.7 Hz, and the rate does not correlate with recording depth (Pearson r = 0.086, p = 0.16; the paper gives r = 0.085, p = 0.16). Under reading (b), the whole trial, the mean is 70.6 +/- 27.4 Hz and the correlation is significant (r = 0.146, p = 0.0167). Within each of the 11 mice with at least 10 cells, the reading (a) correlation is not significant (p >= 0.14).

fig1ijk-modulation-classes¶

Of the 270 first-dataset cells, 60 showed at least 5 Hz facilitation in the CS-US interval (22.2%), 23 showed at least 5 Hz suppression (8.5%), and 187 showed no clear modulation (69.3%).

Source: Results, Characterization of cerebellar IpN neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 1I-K. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Classes as in the Methods (Spike modulation in the last 200 ms of the CS-US interval), on each cell's average trace over its valid trials, with the readings for the baseline correction and for cells meeting both thresholds named in the opening comment. Reproduced when all three counts are within tolerance under one reading.

modulation-absolute-not-rate-dependent¶

Absolute CS-US facilitation did not depend on baseline firing frequency, and absolute suppression only slightly, whereas relative modulation was more clearly linked to firing frequency.

Source: Materials and methods, Spike modulation in the last 200 ms of the CS-US interval, paragraph 1. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Over all 270 first-dataset cells, Spearman correlations of baseline firing frequency with absolute facilitation and suppression (as in fig1ijk-modulation-classes) and with the same values divided by the baseline rate. The paper does not say how suppression is signed, and its printed signs do not plainly fit one convention (r = -0.131 is read as deeper suppression in faster cells, which fits a negative signed value; r = -0.211 for relative suppression fits a positive depth better); readings (a) suppression signed negative, (b) suppression as a positive depth, each applied to both suppression measures. The facilitation test is a claim of absence judged on Spearman at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the facilitation correlation is not significant and the other three are significant, with the printed signs under one reading; the signs found are reported under both.

In [11]:
fr = d1.rate_base
for rd in READINGS:
    f, s = mag(rd, "fac")[df.dset == 1], mag(rd, "sup")[df.dset == 1]
    out = {}
    out["abs fac"] = stats.spearmanr(fr, f)
    out["abs sup, signed negative"] = stats.spearmanr(fr, -s)
    out["abs sup, positive depth"] = stats.spearmanr(fr, s)
    out["rel fac"] = stats.spearmanr(fr, f / fr)
    out["rel sup, signed negative"] = stats.spearmanr(fr, -s / fr)
    out["rel sup, positive depth"] = stats.spearmanr(fr, s / fr)
    print(f"reading {rd}: " + "; ".join(f"{k} r = {v[0]:.3f}, p = {v[1]:.2g}" for k, v in out.items()))

Result: not reproduced. The criterion needs the facilitation test absent and the other three significant with the printed signs under one reading; at most two of the four hold. Absolute facilitation does not depend on the firing frequency under any reading (r = -0.037 to -0.029, p = 0.55 to 0.63), and relative suppression does (reading a, r = -0.207 signed negative, p = 0.00063). Absolute suppression is not related to firing frequency under any reading (|r| <= 0.008, p >= 0.89), where the paper reports r = -0.131, p = 0.03, and relative facilitation is significant only under reading (b) (r = -0.123, p = 0.044, against the paper's -0.378), where reading (a) gives r = -0.003.

fig1m-modulation-grows-with-training¶

The magnitude of CS-US facilitation increased over the course of conditioning (r = 0.413, p = 0.001, n = 60, Spearman); suppression showed a similar but non-significant trend (r = 0.354, p = 0.0972, n = 23).

Source: Results, Characterization of cerebellar IpN neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 1M. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Magnitude as in fig1ijk-modulation-classes (suppression as a positive depth); day is the recording's training day. The paper does not say how recordings after day 6 enter; readings (a) the day values as the dataset codes them, (b) those recordings left out. Reproduced when, under one reading, the facilitation correlation is positive with p < 0.05 and the suppression correlation is positive.

Result: partially reproduced. The criterion's tests hold: with the day codes as given, class reading (a) gives a positive facilitation correlation with training day (r = 0.244, p = 0.029, n = 80) and a positive suppression correlation (r = 0.228, n = 23), and reading (b) also gives a significant facilitation correlation (r = 0.272; the variant a+ gives 0.369). But the effect is weaker than the paper's: both r values under reading (a) are outside the tolerance of 0.413 and 0.354, and no reading puts the facilitation r within 0.372 to 0.454. With the recordings of days 7 to 10 left out, no facilitation correlation is significant (p = 0.11 to 0.33).

fig1no-modulation-more-with-behavior¶

Facilitation and suppression were both more prevalent in recordings with conditioned behavior than without (facilitation 30/103 against 30/167, p = 0.0463; suppression 16/103 against 7/167, p = 0.0025, Chi-square).

Source: Results, Characterization of cerebellar IpN neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 1N,O. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): A 2 by 2 chi-square test for each modulation class. The paper does not say whether Yates' correction was applied; both readings are run. Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with the higher proportion among recordings with behavior under one reading.

The criterion's tests hold: under reading (a) facilitation is more common with behavior (42/111 against 38/159, chi-square p = 0.014, 0.020 with Yates) and so is suppression (16/111 against 7/159, p = 0.0037, 0.0074 with Yates). The suppression counts 16 and 7 equal the paper's, but the facilitation count with behavior is outside 30 +/- 3 under every reading (42, 35 under the variant a+, 44 under b), and the count without behavior is outside it under the claims file's readings (38 and 44) and at its edge, 27, under (a+), so the result holds in part. Reading (b) gives the same direction and loses significance for facilitation with Yates' correction (p = 0.053).

# Trial-by-trial correlations (Methods, Statistics), used by several claims below.
XREAD = ("a", "b", "c")       # per-trial firing rate readings (claims file, opening comment)
YREAD = ("data", "us", "max")  # per-trial CR amplitude: data set's crAmplitude, computed at US onset, CS-US max


def trial_test(cells, xr, yr, sign, rng, boot=True, win2=WIN2):
    """Per-cell correlations of the per-trial rate (reading xr) with CR amplitude (reading yr); counts of
    significant cells in direction `sign` and the opposite one, and the bootstrap p under both null readings."""
    pairs = [(ipn.trial_rates(D, i, None if D["dset"][i] == 1 else win2)[xr], amp_trials(i, yr)) for i in cells]
    r, p, kinds = ipn.trial_corrs(pairs)
    sig = p < 0.05
    n_dir, n_opp = int(np.sum(sig & (np.sign(r) == sign))), int(np.sum(sig & (np.sign(r) == -sign)))
    rs, ps, _ = ipn.trial_corrs(pairs, "spearman")
    out = {"x": xr, "y": yr, "cells": len(cells), "sig": n_dir, "opposite": n_opp,
           "pearson": sum(k == "pearson" for k in kinds),
           "sig, Spearman only": int(np.sum((ps < 0.05) & (np.sign(rs) == sign)))}
    if boot:
        out["p_shuffle"] = ipn.bootstrap_count(pairs, kinds, n_dir, sign, rng, reading="shuffle")[0]
        out["p_random"] = ipn.bootstrap_count(pairs, kinds, n_dir, sign, rng, reading="random")[0]
    return out, r, p, pairs


def lmm_on(cells, sig_mask, pairs, slopes=True, swap=False):
    """Mixed model of CR amplitude (y) on the per-trial rate (x) over the significant cells."""
    xs, ys, gs = [], [], []
    for c, ok, (x, y) in zip(cells, sig_mask, pairs):
        if ok:
            xs += list(x); ys += list(y); gs += [c] * len(x)
    if len(set(gs)) < 2:
        return None
    if swap:
        xs, ys = ys, xs
    return {**ipn.mixedlm(np.array(ys), np.array(xs), np.array(gs), slopes=slopes), "trials": len(xs)}


def lags_for(cells, sign):
    """Lag of the best cross-correlation per cell, for the two estimators (ipn.xcorr_lag: 'xcov' adopted, 'recut'
    variant) and segment readings (a) and (b) of the claims file; Wilcoxon signed rank against 0. Also counts the
    cells whose best lag is at the +/-100 ms edge and those whose curve is flat at its best (the best r within
    0.01 of the 21st best, so that 20 or more lags tie with it)."""
    out = {}
    for est in ("xcov", "recut"):
        for seg_name in ("a, last 200 ms", "b, whole CS-US"):
            lags, flat = [], 0
            for i in cells:
                us = int(D["us"][i])
                seg = (us - 200, us) if seg_name.startswith("a") else (0, us)
                m = np.nanmean(D["sdf"][i], 0)
                e = np.nanmean(D["eyelid"][i], 0)
                lag, r = ipn.xcorr_lag(m, e, t, seg, 100, sign, est)
                lags.append(lag)
                rr = np.sort(sign * r[~np.isnan(r)])
                flat += int(rr[-1] - rr[-21] < 0.01)
            lags = np.array(lags)
            p = stats.wilcoxon(lags).pvalue if np.any(lags != 0) else 1.0
            out[f"{est}, {seg_name}"] = (lags.mean(), lags.std(ddof=1), p, len(lags), int(np.sum(lags > 0)), int(np.sum(lags < 0)),
                                         float(np.median(lags)), int(np.sum(np.abs(lags) == 100)), flat)
    return out


def print_lags(rd, res):
    for k, (mu_, sd_, p, n, npos, nneg, med, edge, flat) in res.items():
        print(f"class {rd}, {k}: lag {mu_:.1f} +/- {sd_:.1f} ms, median {med:.0f} (n = {n}; {npos} positive, {nneg} negative,"
              f" {edge} at the +/-100 ms edge, {flat} flat at the best lag), Wilcoxon p = {p:.3g}")

fig2-s1-correlation-matrix-offsets¶

In spike-eyelid correlation matrices the strongest correlations of facilitation cells lie above the diagonal (spikes leading), at optimal offsets of 80 ms (position) and 20 ms (velocity) in the first dataset and 20 and 10 ms in the second, while suppression cells show offsets of 0 ms for position and -30 and -50 ms for velocity.

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 1; Figure 2C,G,K,O; Figure 2-figure supplement 1A-D. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Tolerance is one matrix step (10 ms), the resolution of the offsets. Per cell, across trials, the correlation of mean eyelid position (or velocity) in each bin with mean spike rate in each bin; r values of the sign opposite to the one of interest set to zero, then averaged over cells (Statistics); the optimal offset is the diagonal offset with the highest mean r in the last 200 ms of the CS-US interval (Figure 2-figure supplement 1 legend). The Results give 20 ms windows at 10 ms steps, the Statistics 20 ms bins (a 100 by 100 matrix); both readings are run. Reproduced when all eight offsets are within tolerance under one reading; partially when only the sign pattern holds (facilitation offsets positive, suppression offsets zero or negative). The paper gives no count of offsets that must match. The quote gives the first-dataset facilitation offsets; the others are in panels B to D of the same legend.

In [20]:
def offsets(cells, sign, step, velocity):
    mats = []
    for i in cells:
        us = int(D["us"][i])
        lo = -200 if D["dset"][i] == 2 else -300
        c, R = ipn.corr_matrix(D["sdf"][i], D["eyelid"][i], t, lo, us + 200, 20, step, velocity)
        mats.append(R)
    us = int(D["us"][cells[0]])
    return ipn.optimal_offset(mats, c, us, sign)

            found[(kind, ds, pv)] = best

                     "all within 10 ms": all(abs(found[k] - expected[k]) <= 10 for k in expected),

fig2e-facilitation-ds2¶

In the second dataset 70 cells showed CS-US facilitation (59.2 +/- 38 Hz) with conditioned behavior, and 49 of them (70%) had significant positive trial-by-trial correlations with CR amplitude.

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 2; Figure 2E,F. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Classes and magnitude as in fig1ijk-modulation-classes, on the second dataset's 102 cells with its own CS-US window (readings in the opening comment), counted among recordings with conditioned behavior (CRs in at least 20% of trials, the paper's criterion throughout, Results, Characterization, paragraph 3), as the text says "in the presence of conditioned behavior". Reproduced when both values are within tolerance under one reading.

fig2f-facilitation-trial-correlations-ds2¶

Of the 70 second-dataset facilitation cells, 49 (70%) showed significant positive trial-by-trial correlations between firing rate and CR amplitude.

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 2; Figure 2F. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): As in fig2b-facilitation-trial-correlations-ds1, on the second dataset. Reproduced when the count is within tolerance under one combination of readings.

rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
res_2f = {}
rows = []
for rd in READINGS:
    for win2 in WINS2:
        cells = list(d2.index[(cls(rd, win2)[df.dset == 2] == "fac") & d2.behav])
        for xr in XREAD:
            for yr in YREAD:
                # the bootstrap is run on the adopted window only, to keep the run short; the 0-200 ms counts are shown
                out, r, p, pairs = trial_test(cells, xr, yr, +1, rng, boot=(win2 == WIN2), win2=win2)
                res_2f[(rd, win2, xr, yr)] = (cells, r, p, pairs)
                rows.append({"class": rd, "window": win2, **out})

fig2f-lmm-ds2¶

In the second dataset a linear mixed model predicts 0.64% more eyelid closure at US onset per 1 Hz of facilitation (p < 0.0001).

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 2; Supplementary file 1, Fig. 2F. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Tolerance is twice the paper's standard error (0.04). As in fig2b-lmm-ds1, over the 49 significant cells. Reproduced when the slope is within tolerance and p < 0.05.

fig2-suppression-properties-ds1¶

The 23 first-dataset suppression cells dropped 11.2 +/- 6 Hz for 70 +/- 44 ms, and suppression magnitude correlated with CR percentage (r = 0.526), CR amplitude at US onset (r = 0.443) and spike irregularity (CV, r = 0.587).

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 3. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Magnitude as a positive depth. CV is the coefficient of variation of interspike intervals; the paper does not give the period, readings (a) the baseline, (b) the whole trial. Reproduced when the three correlations are positive at p < 0.05 and both values are within tolerance under one reading.

for rd in READINGS:
    s = d1[cls(rd)[df.dset == 1] == "sup"]
    m = mag(rd, "sup")[s.index]
    out = f"reading {rd}: n = {len(s)}, magnitude {m.mean():.1f} +/- {m.std():.1f} Hz, duration {s.dur_sup.mean():.1f} +/- {s.dur_sup.std():.1f} ms"
    for nm, col in (("% CRs", "cr_pct"), ("CR amp at US onset (data set)", "amp_us_data"), ("CR amp at US onset (computed)", "amp_us"),
                    ("CV baseline", "cv_base"), ("CV whole trial", "cv_trial")):
        r = stats.spearmanr(m, s[col], nan_policy="omit")
        out += f"; {nm} r = {r[0]:.3f} (p = {r[1]:.3g})"
    print(out)

Result: partially reproduced. Under reading (b) the three correlations are positive and significant (% CRs r = 0.388, p = 0.031; CR amplitude at US onset r = 0.364, p = 0.044; baseline CV r = 0.467, p = 0.008), but the magnitude (9.9 Hz) and duration (53.2 ms) are outside 11.2 +/- 1.12 Hz and 70 +/- 7 ms. Under reading (a) the magnitude (10.3 Hz) and duration (63.6 ms) are within tolerance but only the whole-trial CV correlation is significant. Reading (a+) gives no significant correlation (13 cells).

suppression-smaller-shorter-than-facilitation¶

Compared with facilitation, suppression had lower amplitudes (baseline z-score 5.3 +/- 1.5 against 7.6 +/- 4.7, p = 0.0007) and shorter durations (53 +/- 38.4 against 95.5 +/- 36.2 ms, p = 0.0012, Mann-Whitney U).

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 3. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): The durations printed here (53 and 95.5 ms) differ from those given for all 23 and 60 cells (70 and 104 ms), so the cells compared are not the full classes. Readings (a) all 23 suppression and 60 facilitation cells, (b) the 16 and 30 cells recorded with behavior. Amplitude is the peak absolute baseline z-score in the last 200 ms of the CS-US interval (reading i) or its mean there (reading ii). Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with suppression lower, under one combination of readings; the expected values are reported against tolerance.

Result: reproduced, under class reading (b) over all cells. Suppression has lower peak z-scores (5.46 against 9.14, p = 0.00016) and shorter durations (53.2 against 79.2 ms, p = 0.013). The suppression values (5.46 and 53.2 ms) are within tolerance and the facilitation values (9.14 and 79.2 ms) are not. Under class readings (a) and (a+), and under every reading over the cells with behavior, the duration test is not significant (p = 0.062 to 0.43).

suppression-same-timing-as-facilitation¶

Suppression and facilitation had similar onset times (132 +/- 21.2 against 136.5 +/- 19.9 ms, p = 0.6) and modulation peak times (176 +/- 37.2 against 166 +/- 34.2 ms, p = 0.6).

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 3. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, Mann-Whitney U at p < 0.05, on the cells of the reading that suppression-smaller-shorter-than-facilitation adopts. The paper does not define onset or peak time; the reading, taken from the duration threshold of the Methods (Spike modulation), is onset as the first bin beyond 3 baseline SDs in the CS-US interval held for at least 10 ms, and peak time as the time of the extreme value there. Reproduced when neither test is significant; the differences are reported.

fig2j-suppression-trial-correlations-ds1¶

Of 16 first-dataset suppression cells with conditioned behavior, three (19%) showed significant negative trial-by-trial correlations between firing rate and CR amplitude (bootstrap p < 0.0001), none positive; a mixed model over them estimated 0.27% more closure per Hz of suppression (p = 0.0272).

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 2I,J; Supplementary file 1, Fig. 2J. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Tolerance on the count is one cell (10% is below one); on the slope twice the paper's standard error (0.12). Per-cell correlations, bootstrap and mixed model as in fig2b-facilitation-trial-correlations-ds1 and fig2b-lmm-ds1. Reproduced when the count and the slope are within tolerance and no cell is significantly positive, under one combination of readings.

Result: reproduced. Under class reading (a) with rate reading (a) there are 16 suppression cells with behavior, 4 with significant negative correlations, none positive, and a mixed-model slope of -0.381 % per Hz (p = 0.024), all within tolerance; the bootstrap p is 0.002 or below. fig2l-suppression-no-lead-ds1¶

For first-dataset suppression cells with behavior, cross-correlation offsets between spike and eyelid traces were close to zero on average (6.4 +/- 23 ms, p = 0.2336).

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 3; Figure 2L. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): A claim of absence, judged on the paper's test, a Wilcoxon signed rank test of the lags against zero at p < 0.05, with lags as in fig2d-facilitation-leads-eyelid-ds1 (the cross-correlation taken with the suppression sign of interest, readings as there). Reproduced when the test is not significant; the mean lag is reported.

Result: not reproduced. The Wilcoxon test is significant under every reading and both estimators (p = 0.00013 to 0.0036), so the claimed absence of a lead fails. With the adopted estimator (xcov) the most negative cross-correlation is at a mean lag of 31.2 to 34.0 ms, with at most one cell at the +/-100 ms edge; the re-cut Pearson variant gives 48.0 to 70.9 ms, with 7 to 11 cells at the edge.

fig2n-suppression-ds2¶

In the second dataset 16 cells showed CS-US suppression (12.1 +/- 5 Hz) with conditioned behavior; 8 had significant negative trial-by-trial correlations with CR amplitude (bootstrap p < 0.0001), and a mixed model estimated 1.01% more closure per Hz of deeper suppression (p < 0.0001).

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 4; Figure 2M,N; Supplementary file 1, Fig. 2N. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Tolerance on the slope is twice the paper's standard error (0.1); on the count one cell. Here the firing rate is "relative"; readings (a) the trial rate minus the baseline mean, (b) as in the first-dataset claims. Supplementary file 1 says this model had random intercepts only. Reproduced when the four values are within tolerance under one combination of readings.

    for win2 in WINS2 + ("0-212",):

expected: 16 +/- 1.6 cells, 12.1 +/- 1.21 Hz, 8 +/- 1 significant, slope -1.01 +/- 0.2

Result: partially reproduced. Negative trial-by-trial correlations and a negative slope are present under every combination, but no combination of the claims file's windows and readings puts all four values within tolerance. The magnitude (10.9 to 11.7 Hz) is within tolerance throughout; the cell count is 11 to 21 (none of the claims file's readings gives 15 to 17; class (a), 0-200 ms gives 14, just below 14.4); rate reading (a) gives 6 or 7 significant cells with a slope near -0.6 % per Hz, rate reading (c) 2 or 3 cells with a slope near -1.0. Most of the random-intercept fits have a singular random-effects covariance (fit-ok column), including the -0.620 of class (a), rate (a). The variant window 0-212 ms, which the verifier asked for, gives 16 cells under class (a) but 5 significant cells and a slope of -0.60, so it does not put all four values within tolerance either. Class (a), 0-200 ms, rate (a) with the data set's CR amplitude gives 7 significant cells, within 8 +/- 1 (bootstrap p below 1/500), among 14 cells, just below 14.4, with a slope of -0.603 from a singular fit (-0.592 from the clean fit with the computed CR amplitude), outside -1.01 +/- 0.2: the effect is present and some of its values are within tolerance.

ds2-stronger-facilitation-same-suppression¶

The second dataset showed stronger facilitation than the first (59.2 +/- 38.1 against 30.1 +/- 25.3 Hz, p = 0.0009), with high CR performance (86.2 +/- 17.3% CRs, CR amplitude 43.5 +/- 17%), while suppression did not differ (11.9 +/- 5 against 12.9 +/- 6.4 Hz, p = 0.864).

Source: Results, IpN facilitation but not suppression can drive conditioned eyelid behavior, paragraph 4. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): The first-dataset facilitation mean (30.1 Hz) differs from that of all 60 cells (22.5 Hz); readings for the groups are (a) the cells with behavior (30 and 70 facilitation, 16 and 16 suppression), (b) all cells of each class. Facilitation is reproduced when the Mann-Whitney test gives p < 0.05 with the second dataset higher; suppression is a claim of absence judged on the same test. Reproduced when both hold and the expected values are within tolerance under one reading; partially when only the tests hold.

Criterion (claims file): The count of 87 is 70 plus 17 (85% of 102). Classes as in fig1ijk-modulation-classes on the second dataset. Reproduced when both counts are within tolerance under one reading.

fig3-optogenetic-inhibition-abolishes-crs¶

Optogenetic stimulation of Purkinje cell terminals over the IpN during the CS-US interval disabled conditioned eyelid responses in virtually all stimulated trials in each of three trained L7cre-Ai27 mice (all p < 0.0001).

Source: Results, Optogenetic inhibition of IpN eliminates CRs, paragraph 1; Figure 3B,C. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Per mouse, eyelid closure at US onset in the 10 stimulated against the 40 unstimulated trials of its 50-trial session (Methods, Optogenetics), Mann-Whitney U. Reproduced when all three mice give p < 0.05 with lower closure in stimulated trials.

# CS transients: the four readings of the threshold (claims file), the two windows (Methods 50-125 ms,
# Results overview 50-130 ms), and where the rebound is looked for (within the window, or up to 50 ms after
# the trough, "+50"); see ipn.CS_WINDOWS.
CSREAD = [f"{a}/{b}" for a in ("mean", "drop") for b in ("trough", "mean")]


CSWIN = list(ipn.CS_WINDOWS)  # "125", "130", "125+50", "130+50": window end, and rebound within 50 ms after the trough


def cs_col(kind, rd, end="125"):
    return df[f"cs{kind}_{rd}_{end}"].astype(bool)


def fisher(a, b):
    """Two-sided Fisher exact test of the 2x2 table of boolean series a (rows) and b (columns)."""
    tab = [[int((a & b).sum()), int((a & ~b).sum())], [int((~a & b).sum()), int((~a & ~b).sum())]]
    return stats.fisher_exact(tab)[1], tab

fig4b-cs-pause-ds1¶

In the first dataset seven cells showed a CS pause at 88 +/- 12 ms after the CS, five of which also showed CS-US facilitation (71.4%, against 55/263 or 21% of the other cells, p = 0.0006, Fisher's test).

Source: Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 1; Figure 4B,E. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Tolerance on the count is one cell. CS pause as in the opening comment (Methods, CS-responses), the four readings of the threshold run. Reproduced when the count and latency are within tolerance and Fisher's exact test (two-sided) gives p < 0.05 with facilitation more common among CS pause cells, under one reading.

Result: partially reproduced. No reading of the claims file, with the rebound within the window, gives 6 to 8 CS pause cells. Under the drop/mean reading, 9 cells (50-125 ms) have a CS pause at 84.6 +/- 11.3 ms, 8 of them with facilitation (Fisher p = 0.0003 to 0.0007), so the association holds with one cell more than the tolerance. The mean/trough and mean/mean readings give 4 and 3 cells without a significant association, and drop/trough gives 23. With the rebound looked for up to 50 ms after the trough, mean/trough gives 6 cells (within tolerance) but at 98.7 ms, outside 88 +/- 8.8 ms, with 2 of them facilitating (Fisher p = 0.62 to 1).

fig4c-cs-pause-ds2¶

In the second dataset 41 of 102 cells showed CS pauses, and these were more likely to show CS-US facilitation than cells without (39/41 against 31/61, p < 0.0001, Fisher's test).

Source: Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4C,F. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): As in fig4b-cs-pause-ds1, on the second dataset.

Result: partially reproduced. CS pause cells are more often facilitating under every reading (Fisher p = 1.2e-07 to 0.034) except mean/trough with the 50-130 ms window and the 50 ms rebound (p = 0.050 to 0.080). Under the mean/trough readings the count (37 or 40) is within 41 +/- 4.1, but only 31 or 32 of them facilitate, below 39 +/- 3.9; the drop readings give 43 or 44 facilitating cells among 47 to 56 pause cells, above the count's tolerance. The class window (12-212 or 0-200 ms) changes the facilitating count by at most one cell.

fig4g-cs-pause-latency-cr-latency¶

Across cells, CS pause latency correlated with CR latency, in both datasets combined (n = 45, r = 0.582, p < 0.0001) and in the second dataset alone (n = 41, r = 0.403, p = 0.0089).

Source: Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4G. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Pause latency is the time of the trough of the cell's average trace. CR latency is, per the Figure 4G legend, the latency at which the CR passes 5% eyelid closure (reading a, on the average eyelid trace; reading b, the mean of trial values over CR trials); the Methods' CR onset (start of continuous positive velocity) is reading c. The 45 cells are those with both a CS pause and CRs. Reproduced when both correlations are positive at p < 0.05 under one reading, and the r values are reported against tolerance.

Result: reproduced. Under the mean/trough threshold with CR latency reading (b), both correlations are positive and significant (both datasets r = 0.385, p = 0.016, n = 39; second dataset r = 0.347, p = 0.035, n = 37), and the drop readings give stronger ones (both datasets up to r = 0.571). The r values are below the paper's 0.582 and 0.403 except under drop/trough with reading (b) (0.560 and 0.389, within tolerance). With CR latency reading (a), the mean/trough threshold gives no significant correlation.

fig4s1-cs-peak-cells¶

Four first-dataset cells showed a transient increase in firing at the CS pause latency; two of them showed CS-US suppression (50%, against 21/266 or 7.9% of other cells, p = 0.0021, Fisher's test); no such cell was seen in the second dataset.

Source: Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 4-figure supplement 1A,B. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Tolerance on the first-dataset count is one cell; the second-dataset count is the paper's "not observed in any", so it carries none. CS peak as in the Methods (CS-responses), the four readings of the threshold run. Reproduced when the counts are within tolerance and Fisher's exact test gives p < 0.05 with suppression more common among CS peak cells, under one reading.

Result: reproduced. Under the drop/mean reading, 4 first-dataset cells and no second-dataset cell show a CS peak, and 3 of the 4 show suppression (Fisher p = 0.0021 under class reading a, 0.0003 and 0.0051 under a+ and b). The mean/mean readings with the 50 ms rebound give 5 and 0 cells, 3 of the 5 suppressing (p = 0.0118 under class b). The other readings give 2 to 59 first-dataset cells and up to 57 second-dataset cells.

fig4s1-cs-peak-suppression-not-different¶

Suppression cells with a CS peak did not differ from other suppression cells in minimum CS-US spike rate (-33.6 +/- 15.4 against -34 +/- 9.6 Hz, p = 1), spike rate velocity (p = 0.2096) or recording depth (p = 0.7348).

Source: Figure 4-figure supplement 1C-E; Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 3. Data: with_inputs.

Criterion (claims file): A claim of absence, judged on the paper's tests, Mann-Whitney U at p < 0.05, between the two CS peak cells with suppression and the other 21 suppression cells. Minimum spike rate relative to baseline in the CS-US interval; velocity as in the opening comment; recording depth from Source data 1 (opening comment). Reproduced when none of the three tests is significant; the differences are reported.

Depth from Source data 1 (see source-data-1-link).

fig4h-transient-responses-after-day-3¶

In the first dataset none of the 11 cells with a transient response at the CS-related complex spike latency (CS pause or CS peak) was recorded before day 4 of training (0/99 on days 1 to 3 against 11/171 later, p = 0.0058, Fisher's test).

Source: Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 4; Figure 4H. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Reproduced when no CS pause or CS peak cell is recorded on days 1 to 3 and Fisher's exact test gives p < 0.05.

Result: reproduced, under the drop/mean reading (50-125 ms). None of the 13 cells with a CS pause or peak is recorded on days 1 to 3 (0/99 against 13/171, Fisher p = 0.0026); there are 99 first-dataset recordings on days 1 to 3. Under the other readings either 1 to 27 transient cells fall on days 1 to 3, or none do but the test is not significant (mean/mean without the 50 ms rebound, 0/99 against 5/171, p = 0.16).

fig5cd-cs-pause-faster-facilitation-ds1¶

In the first dataset, facilitation cells with a CS pause had higher CS-US increases in firing rate (41.5 +/- 33.1 against 15.2 +/- 8.9 Hz, p = 0.0013) and higher maximum spike rate velocities (4.9 +/- 1.6 against 1.4 +/- 0.5 Hz/ms, p = 0.0002) than those without.

Source: Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 5C,D. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Groups are the 5 and 55 facilitation cells with and without a CS pause (Figure 5A,B). The Figure 5C legend says "Maximum spike rate in the CS-US interval" and the text "CR-related increases in firing rate"; neither gives the reference, so the readings are (a) the maximum of the average trace in the CS-US interval minus the baseline mean, (b) the CS-US facilitation of fig1ijk-modulation-classes. Velocity as in the opening comment, within the CS-US interval. Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with CS pause cells higher; the values are reported against tolerance.

def fig5(ds, wins=(WIN2,)):
    sub = df[df.dset == ds]
    rows = []
    for end in CSWIN:
        for rd in CSREAD:
            for crd, win2 in [(c_, w) for c_ in READINGS for w in wins]:
                f = sub[(cls(crd, win2) == "fac")[sub.index]]
                cp = cs_col("pause", rd, end)[f.index]
                a, b = f[cp], f[~cp]
                if len(a) == 0:
                    continue
                ma, mb = mag(crd, "fac", win2)[a.index], mag(crd, "fac", win2)[b.index]
                rows.append({"window": end, "threshold": rd, "class": crd + ("" if ds == 1 else f", {win2}"), "n pause": len(a), "n other": len(b),
                             "(a) max-base pause": f"{a.max_csus.mean():.1f} +/- {a.max_csus.std():.1f}",
                             "other": f"{b.max_csus.mean():.1f} +/- {b.max_csus.std():.1f}", "p (a)": fmt(ipn.mwu(a.max_csus, b.max_csus), 4),
                             "(b) fac pause": f"{ma.mean():.1f}", "other ": f"{mb.mean():.1f}", "p (b)": fmt(ipn.mwu(ma, mb), 4),
                             "velocity pause": f"{a.vel_max.mean():.2f} +/- {a.vel_max.std():.2f}",
                             "other  ": f"{b.vel_max.mean():.2f} +/- {b.vel_max.std():.2f}", "p vel": fmt(ipn.mwu(a.vel_max, b.vel_max), 4)})
    print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Result: reproduced, under the drop readings with class reading (b) or the variant (a+). Under class (b), with the 50-125 ms window, the 8 facilitation cells with a CS pause have a higher maximum rate than the 80 without (reading a, 94.4 against 48.1 Hz, p = 0.014; reading b, 44.4 against 15.4 Hz, p = 0.0098) and a higher maximum velocity (8.91 against 5.77 Hz/ms, p = 0.046). The reading (b) rates are within the tolerance of 41.5 and 15.2 Hz; the velocities are outside that of 4.9 and 1.4 Hz/ms, on a scale two to four times the paper's. Under the variant (a+) the 7 CS pause cells against 55 give 105.7 against 52.8 Hz (p = 0.0028), 45.0 against 16.4 Hz (p = 0.014) and 9.97 against 5.58 Hz/ms (p = 0.004). Under the mean readings only 2 facilitation cells have a pause and no test is significant.

fig5hi-cs-pause-faster-facilitation-ds2¶

In the second dataset, maximum facilitation was not significantly higher in cells with a CS pause (65.1 +/- 39.5 against 51.7 +/- 35.4 Hz, p = 0.1594), but maximum spike rate velocity was (5.6 +/- 2.5 against 3.6 +/- 1.5 Hz/ms, p = 0.0004).

Source: Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 5H,I. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): As in fig5cd-cs-pause-faster-facilitation-ds1, on the 39 and 31 second-dataset facilitation cells. The facilitation comparison is a claim of absence, judged on the same Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the facilitation test is not significant and the velocity test is, with CS pause cells higher.

Result: reproduced. Under every threshold reading and class window the maximum facilitation does not differ (p = 0.24 to 0.97); under the drop readings the velocity is higher in CS pause cells (9.35 against 5.76 Hz/ms, p = 0.0002, class a), and under the mean readings only with class (b) on the 12-212 ms window (p = 0.044; 0.055 on 0-200 ms). The velocities are outside the tolerance of 5.6 and 3.6 Hz/ms. Under the mean/trough reading, the one whose count fits fig4c-cs-pause-ds2, the velocity test holds only with class (b) on the 12-212 ms window.

fig5ej-cs-pause-cells-shallower¶

CS pause cells were recorded less deeply than cells without, in the first (1840 +/- 320 against 2130 +/- 350 um, p = 0.0298) and second dataset (2350 +/- 140 against 2450 +/- 211 um, p = 0.0372).

Source: Results, CS-related transient spike pauses and subsequent rapid excitation in IpN neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 5E,J. Data: with_inputs.

Criterion (claims file): Groups as in Figure 5 (facilitation cells with and without a CS pause, Figure 5E,J legend). Recording depth from Source data 1 (opening comment). Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with CS pause cells shallower.

Groups as in fig5cd-cs-pause-faster-facilitation-ds1 and fig5hi-cs-pause-faster-facilitation-ds2, under every threshold, window and class reading. Depth from Source data 1 (see source-data-1-link), which gives none for the second dataset.

rows = []
for ds in (1, 2):
    sub = df[df.dset == ds]
    for end in CSWIN:
        for rd in CSREAD:
            for crd in READINGS:
                f = sub[(cls(crd) == "fac")[sub.index]]
                cp = cs_col("pause", rd, end)[f.index]
                a, b = f[cp].depth.dropna(), f[~cp].depth.dropna()
                rows.append({"set": ds, "window": end, "threshold": rd, "class": crd, "n pause": int(cp.sum()), "n other": int((~cp).sum()),
                             "with depth": f"{len(a)}/{len(b)}",
                             "depth pause": f"{a.mean():.0f} +/- {a.std():.0f}" if len(a) else "-",
                             "depth other": f"{b.mean():.0f} +/- {b.std():.0f}" if len(b) else "-",
                             "p": fmt(ipn.mwu(a, b), 4) if len(a) and len(b) else np.nan})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

fig5s1-model-timing¶

IpN neurons modeled from Purkinje cell simple spike suppression align better with recorded facilitation cells without a CS pause, with earlier onset (73 +/- 19 against 88 +/- 25 ms, p = 0.0098) and peak times (144 +/- 55 against 171 +/- 43 ms, p = 0.0221), and lower peak amplitude and velocity than CS pause cells.

(2015) and the model of Figure 5-source data 1 (Methods, Simple spike-based model of IpN neurons), neither of which the paper deposits with the IpN data. Values in baseline z-scores (z/ms for velocity). Reproduced when the model's facilitation onset and peak are earlier than those of cells without a CS pause at p < 0.05 and CS pause cells exceed both in peak amplitude at p < 0.05.

In [49]:
def peak_trials(i, which):
    """Per-trial US response values: maximum (first or second peak) or minimum (pause) absolute rate in a 30 ms
    window centred on the cell's average peak or pause time (Methods, US-responses)."""
    us = int(D["us"][i])
    if which == "peak1":
        return ipn.trial_extreme(D["sdf"][i], t, us + df.peak1_t[i], "max")
    if which == "peak2":
        return ipn.trial_extreme(D["sdf"][i], t, us + df.peak2_t[i], "max")
    return ipn.trial_extreme(D["sdf"][i], t, us + df.pause_t[i], "min")


def us_trial_test(cells, which, yr, sign, rng):
    pairs = [(amp_trials(i, yr), peak_trials(i, which)) for i in cells]
    r, p, kinds = ipn.trial_corrs(pairs)
    sig = p < 0.05
    n_dir, n_opp = int(np.sum(sig & (np.sign(r) == sign))), int(np.sum(sig & (np.sign(r) == -sign)))
    pb_s = ipn.bootstrap_count(pairs, kinds, n_dir, sign, rng, reading="shuffle")[0]
    pb_r = ipn.bootstrap_count(pairs, kinds, n_dir, sign, rng, reading="random")[0]
    rs, ps, _ = ipn.trial_corrs(pairs, "spearman")
    return {"cells": len(cells), "sig": n_dir, "opposite": n_opp, "p_shuffle": pb_s, "p_random": pb_r,
            "sig, Spearman only": int(np.sum((ps < 0.05) & (np.sign(rs) == sign)))}, r, p, pairs

Criterion (claims file): Trial values as in the Methods (US-responses), the maximum in a 30 ms window centred on the cell's average peak time, against CR amplitude. Supplementary file 1 says the model used 15 cells where the Results say 13; the model is fitted on the significant cells found here. Slope tolerance is twice the paper's standard error (0.36). Reproduced when the counts and slope are within tolerance and the bootstrap p is below 0.05, under one combination of readings.

The CS transient claims under one reading at a time¶

Each CS transient claim above is judged under any of the readings, as its criterion says. This table holds each reading fixed (threshold reading and window) and says, for each claim, whether its criterion is met under that reading with any class reading (and, in the second dataset, either window of the claims file). fig4b and fig4c need the count and latency or the count of facilitation cells within tolerance and the Fisher test; fig4s1 needs both counts and the Fisher test; fig4h needs no transient on days 1 to 3 and the Fisher test; fig4g needs both correlations positive at p < 0.05 under a CR latency reading; fig5cd needs both tests (either facilitation reading) and fig5hi the absence and the velocity test; cs-pause-cells-have-us-pause needs the Fisher test, and its count of 6 +/- 1 is shown beside it. The "+50" windows are this attempt's variant, not readings of the claims file.

In [56]:
def met_by_reading(end, rd):
    sub1, sub2 = df.dset == 1, df.dset == 2
    cp, pk = cs_col("pause", rd, end), cs_col("peak", rd, end)
    lat = df[f"cspause_t_{rd}_{end}"]
    out = {}
    ok = False
    for crd in READINGS:
        p, tab = fisher(cp[sub1], (cls(crd) == "fac")[sub1])
        ok |= bool(6 <= cp[sub1].sum() <= 8 and abs(lat[sub1 & cp].mean() - 88) <= 8.8 and p < 0.05 and tab[0][0] / max(cp[sub1].sum(), 1) > tab[1][0] / (tab[1][0] + tab[1][1]))
    out["fig4b"] = ok
    ok = False
    for crd in READINGS:
        for w in WINS2:
            fac2 = (cls(crd, w) == "fac")[sub2]
            p, tab = fisher(cp[sub2], fac2)
            ok |= bool(36.9 <= cp[sub2].sum() <= 45.1 and 35.1 <= tab[0][0] <= 42.9 and p < 0.05)
    out["fig4c"] = ok
    ok = False
    for crl in ("crlat_a", "crlat_b", "crlat_c"):
        a, b = cp & df[crl].notna() & df.behav, cp & df[crl].notna() & df.behav & sub2
        if a.sum() > 2 and b.sum() > 2:
            r1, r2 = stats.pearsonr(lat[a], df[crl][a]), stats.pearsonr(lat[b], df[crl][b])
            ok |= bool(r1[0] > 0 and r1[1] < 0.05 and r2[0] > 0 and r2[1] < 0.05)
    out["fig4g"] = ok
    ok = False
    for crd in READINGS:
        p, tab = fisher(pk[sub1], (cls(crd) == "sup")[sub1])
        ok |= bool(3 <= pk[sub1].sum() <= 5 and pk[sub2].sum() == 0 and p < 0.05 and tab[0][0] > 0)
    out["fig4s1"] = ok
    tr, early = (cp | pk)[sub1], d1.day <= 3
    p, tab = fisher(tr, early)
    out["fig4h"] = bool(tab[0][0] == 0 and p < 0.05)
    for ds, key in ((1, "fig5cd"), (2, "fig5hi")):
        ok = False
        for crd in READINGS:
            for w in (WINS2 if ds == 2 else (WIN2,)):
                f = df[(df.dset == ds) & (cls(crd, w) == "fac")]
                a, b = f[cp[f.index]], f[~cp[f.index]]
                if len(a) == 0:
                    continue
                pv = ipn.mwu(a.vel_max, b.vel_max)
                vel = pv < 0.05 and a.vel_max.mean() > b.vel_max.mean()
                if ds == 1:
                    for col_a, col_b in ((a.max_csus, b.max_csus), (mag(crd, "fac")[a.index], mag(crd, "fac")[b.index])):
                        ok |= bool(vel and ipn.mwu(col_a, col_b) < 0.05 and col_a.mean() > col_b.mean())
                else:
                    for col_a, col_b in ((a.max_csus, b.max_csus), (mag(crd, "fac", w)[a.index], mag(crd, "fac", w)[b.index])):
                        ok |= bool(vel and ipn.mwu(col_a, col_b) >= 0.05)
        out[key] = ok
    p, tab = fisher(cp[sub1], d1.pause)
    out["cs-us pause (test)"] = bool(p < 0.05 and tab[0][0] / max(cp[sub1].sum(), 1) > tab[1][0] / (tab[1][0] + tab[1][1]))
    out["cs-us pause count"] = f"{tab[0][0]}/{int(cp[sub1].sum())}"
    return out


rows = [{"window": end, "threshold": rd, **met_by_reading(end, rd)} for end in CSWIN for rd in CSREAD]

tab["criteria met (of 8)"] = tab[crit].sum(axis=1)
print(tab.to_string(index=False))
print("claims whose criterion is met under at least one reading:", {k: bool(tab[k].any()) for k in crit})

Across readings. No single reading meets the criteria of all eight CS transient tests. The drop/mean reading with the 50-125 ms window meets five (fig4g, fig4s1, fig4h, fig5cd, fig5hi) and fails fig4b (9 cells against 7 +/- 1), fig4c and the CS-US pause test; the mean readings, whose fig4c counts come closest, meet two or three. The per-claim outcomes below and in the record are each judged under any reading, as the criteria say; as a set, the CS transient results reproduce under no single reading.

fig6b-us-peak-pause-overlap¶

US peaks and pauses overlapped; a third of the cells with one response also showed the other (77 of 239, 32.2%), leaving 134 with a peak only, 28 with a pause only and 31 with neither.

Source: Results, IpN responses to the US, paragraph 3; Figure 6A,B,E,F legend. Data: dataset.

Judged on the expected values alone.

fig6g-us-response-depth¶

Cells with only a US pause lay more dorsally (1939 +/- 299 um) than cells with only a US peak (2182 +/- 373 um), with cells showing both in between (2075 +/- 322 um; p = 0.0025, Kruskal-Wallis).

Source: Results, IpN responses to the US, paragraph 3; Figure 6G. Data: with_inputs.

Criterion (claims file): Kruskal-Wallis over the three groups, recording depth from Source data 1 (opening comment). Reproduced when p < 0.05 and the mean depths are ordered pause only, both, peak only, from shallow to deep.

Groups as in fig6b-us-peak-pause-overlap. Depth from Source data 1 (see source-data-1-link).

In [58]:
groups = {"pause only": d1[~d1.peak1 & d1.pause], "both": d1[d1.peak1 & d1.pause], "peak only": d1[d1.peak1 & ~d1.pause]}
for nm, g in groups.items():
    print(f"{nm}: n = {len(g)}, depth {g.depth.mean():.0f} +/- {g.depth.std():.0f} um, from {g.mouse.nunique()} mice")
h, p = stats.kruskal(*[g.depth for g in groups.values()])
print(f"Kruskal-Wallis H = {h:.2f}, p = {p:.3g}")
for a, b in (("pause only", "both"), ("both", "peak only"), ("pause only", "peak only")):
    print(f"  {a} vs {b}: MWU p = {ipn.mwu(groups[a].depth, groups[b].depth):.3g}")
# Variant: depth relative to the mean depth of the mouse's first-dataset cells, as depth differs by mouse (data check above).
rel = d1.depth - d1.groupby("mouse").depth.transform("mean")
gs = [rel[g.index] for g in groups.values()]
print(f"variant, depth relative to the mouse's mean: means {[round(g.mean()) for g in gs]} um, Kruskal-Wallis p = {stats.kruskal(*gs)[1]:.3g}")
# The US pause and second peak turnaround span is a choice (see us-pause-prevalence); the groups under 20 and 45 ms.
for span in (20, 45):
    pk, pa = [], []
    for i in d1.index:
        m = np.nanmean(D["sdf"][i], 0)
        z = (m - df.mu[i]) / df.sd[i]
        u = ipn.us_responses(z, m, t, int(D["us"][i]), df.mu[i], turn_span=span)
        pk.append(u["peak1"])
        pa.append(u["pause"])
    pk, pa = np.array(pk), np.array(pa)
    gs = [d1.depth[~pk & pa], d1.depth[pk & pa], d1.depth[pk & ~pa]]
    print(f"turnaround within {span} ms: n {[len(g) for g in gs]}, mean depth {[round(g.mean()) for g in gs]} um,"
          f" Kruskal-Wallis p = {stats.kruskal(*gs)[1]:.3g}")

Result: reproduced. Cells with only a US pause lie shallowest (1920 +/- 290 um, n = 23), cells with both in between (2061 +/- 323 um, n = 76) and cells with only a US peak deepest (2186 +/- 364 um, n = 138); all three means are within tolerance and the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p = 0.00067 (paper 0.0025). The order and significance hold with depth taken relative to each mouse's mean (p = 0.0057) and with turnaround spans of 20 and 45 ms (p = 0.00067 and 0.00052).

us-pause-declines-with-training¶

The US pause became less common and weaker with training; 47.1% of cells (66/140) on the first four training days had one against 30% (39/130) later (p = 0.0057), and magnitudes were lower from day 5 (-13 +/- 30.3 against -28.8 +/- 30.4 Hz, p = 0.0018).

Source: Results, IpN responses to the US, paragraph 3; Figure 6C, right panel. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Chi-square with and without Yates' correction (not stated). Magnitude is the minimum in 16 to 45 ms after the US, relative to the last 50 ms of the CS-US interval (reading a, as in the Figure 6C legend, which makes a different comparison, pre- against post+) or to the baseline mean (reading b; the text does not give the reference for the day comparison), over (i) all cells or (ii) US pause cells only. Reproduced when both tests give p < 0.05 with early days showing more and deeper pauses, under one reading.

The counts 140 and 68 are within tolerance, but 31 later-day pause cells is below 39 +/- 3.9. Over the US pause cells alone the depth does not differ (p = 0.27 and 0.31).

fig6h-us-pause-trial-correlations¶

Trial by trial, 4 of 41 recordings with a US pause and at least 20% CRs showed deeper pauses in trials with worse behavior (bootstrap p = 0.0017).

Source: Results, IpN responses to the US, paragraph 3; Figure 6H; Supplementary file 1, Fig. 6H. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Pause value per trial is the minimum firing rate in a 30 ms window centred on the cell's average pause time. The legend gives n = 37 where the text gives 41; both are reported. Supplementary file 1 fits a model "across IpN cells" with a T-test and no stated random effects; the slope tolerance is twice its standard error (0.06). Reproduced when the count of significant cells is within tolerance and the bootstrap p is below 0.05.

In [60]:
import statsmodels.api as sm
rng = np.random.default_rng(64)
cells41 = list(d1.index[d1.pause & d1.behav])
for yr in ("data", "us", "max"):
    out, r, p, pairs = us_trial_test(cells41, "pause", yr, +1, rng)
    sig = (p < 0.05) & (r > 0)
    xs = np.concatenate([x for (x, y), s in zip(pairs, sig) if s] + [np.array([])])
    ys = np.concatenate([y for (x, y), s in zip(pairs, sig) if s] + [np.array([])])
    ols = sm.OLS(ys, sm.add_constant(xs)).fit() if len(xs) > 2 else None
    print(f"CR amplitude {yr}: {out}" + (f"; linear model pause rate on closure: slope {ols.params[1]:.2f} +/- {ols.bse[1]:.2f} Hz per %,"
                                         f" T({int(ols.df_resid)}) = {ols.tvalues[1]:.2f}" if ols is not None else ""))
print("expected: 41 +/- 4.1 cells (37 in the legend), 4 +/- 1 significant, bootstrap p < 0.05")

Result: partially reproduced. The criterion's count and bootstrap hold with the data set's CR amplitude or the CS-US maximum: 4 of 35 US pause cells with behavior have significant positive correlations (bootstrap p = 0.014 to 0.020; with the CS-US maximum, 4 cells, p = 0.004 to 0.010). With the CR amplitude computed at the stated US onset, 2 cells (p = 0.20 to 0.23). But 3 cells are significant in the opposite direction, the cell count (35) is outside 41 +/- 4.1 (and below the legend's 37), and the linear-model slope (0.37 Hz per %) is outside 0.66 +/- 0.12, so the result holds in part. Source data 1's CR flags give 33 US pause cells with behavior (Source data 1 comparison, above).

fig7-second-us-peak¶

In the first dataset 83 cells showed a second US peak, peaking at 46 +/- 7 ms after the US with magnitudes of 61.4 +/- 28.3 Hz (39.4%).

Source: Results, US pauses are followed by fast excitatory responses in IpN neurons after conditioning, paragraph 1; Figure 7A. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Second peak as in the Methods (US-responses), 31 to 60 ms after the US. 39.4% matches 83 of the 211 US peak cells, not of 270, and the Figure 7B legend counts cells with both a first and a second peak; readings (a) second peaks in any cell, (b) only in cells with a first peak. Reproduced when the count and peak time are within tolerance, and the magnitude, under one reading.

fig7-second-us-peak-dynamics¶

The second US peak was stronger in recordings with poor behavior (26 +/- 32 against 13 +/- 26 Hz, p = 0.025) and did not decline over training (r = 0.102, p = 0.13, n = 224); across recordings with poor CRs it grew over training (r = 0.287, p = 0.0007, n = 138), from 16 +/- 28.3 Hz on days 1 to 4 to 46.5 +/- 33 Hz later (p = 0.0001), with higher spike rate velocity later (0.55 +/- 0.32 against 0.77 +/- 0.45 Hz/ms, p = 0.0072).

Source: Results, US pauses are followed by fast excitatory responses in IpN neurons after conditioning, paragraph 1; Figure 7D,E. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Amplitude is the maximum 30 to 60 ms after the US (the text) relative to the last 50 ms of the CS-US interval or to baseline (both run), for all cells. Poor behavior is fewer than 20% CRs. The days 1 to 4 against later comparison (121 plus 46) covers the 167 recordings without behavior (fig1l-cells-with-behavior), and the Figure 7E legend restricts the velocity comparison to recordings without behavior as well, so both are run on them. The other n values (224 for all recordings, 138 for poor behavior) match neither 270 nor 167, and the paper does not say which recordings are left out; the counts found are reported. The text's panel citations do not match the Figure 7 legend (which puts the velocity comparison in 7E); the text's values are used. The decline is a claim of absence judged on Spearman at p < 0.05. Reproduced when the four positive tests give p < 0.05 in the printed direction and the all-recordings correlation is not significant, under one reading.

Result: partially reproduced. Measured from the last 50 ms, the second peak is larger with poor behavior (30.7 against 18.7 Hz, p = 0.011), does not change with day over all 270 recordings (r = 0.026, p = 0.68), grows with day among the 159 poor-behavior recordings (r = 0.202, p = 0.011) and is larger after day 4 among them (47.1 against 24.6 Hz, p = 0.0009); the velocity comparison is not significant (3.54 against 4.49 Hz/ms, p = 0.053). Measured from baseline, the poor against good comparison is not significant (p = 0.083). The later-day amplitude (47.1 Hz) is within tolerance and the early one (24.6 Hz) is not. The velocity is the claims file's reading (first difference of the 1 ms spike density), whose values are several times the paper's, so the one failed test uses a measure on a different scale from the paper's.

fig7c-second-peak-cells-lower-cr¶

Cells with a second US peak showed lower CR amplitudes at US onset than cells without, in the first (p < 0.0001) and second dataset (31.3 +/- 15.9 against 44.9 +/- 16.6% closure, p = 0.021); in the second dataset only 9 cells (8.8%) had a first US peak, 24 (23.5%) a US pause and 11 (10.8%) a second US peak.

Source: Results, US pauses are followed by fast excitatory responses in IpN neurons after conditioning, paragraph 2; Figure 7C legend. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): US responses as in the Methods, on paired trials. Per cell, the mean CR amplitude at US onset. Reproduced when both Mann-Whitney tests give p < 0.05 with lower CR amplitude in second peak cells and the counts are within tolerance.

fig7b-first-second-peak-correlated¶

The amplitudes of the first and second US peaks were correlated trial by trial; a mixed model over 14 cells gives 0.31 Hz of second peak per Hz of first peak (p < 0.0001).

Source: Results, US pauses are followed by fast excitatory responses in IpN neurons after conditioning, paragraph 1; Figure 7B legend; Supplementary file 1, Fig. 7B. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): Per cell among the cells with both peaks, the trial-by-trial correlation of first and second peak values (30 ms windows centred on the average peak times); mixed model over the significant cells, tolerance twice the paper's standard error (0.04). The paper reports no test of the count of significant cells (the Figure 7B pie chart only shows it), so none is required. Reproduced when the slope is positive and within tolerance with p < 0.05 and the count is within tolerance.

Result: partially reproduced. First and second peaks are correlated trial by trial, positively and significantly (mixed-model p = 6e-61), but the values are far from the paper's: 58 of 105 cells are significant (against 14 +/- 1.4) and the mixed-model slope is 0.617 Hz/Hz (against 0.31 +/- 0.08). In 40 of the 105 cells the two 30 ms windows overlap, which inflates the correlations; among the other 65, 24 are significant.

us-only-trials-ds2¶

In 25 second-dataset cells with US-only trials, the first US peak (10/25) and US pause (10/25) were more common than in paired trials, and the second US peak was most common (18 cells, 72%) and larger than the first (94.6 +/- 82.9 against 27.8 +/- 48.7 Hz, p = 0.0012).

Source: Results, US pauses are followed by fast excitatory responses in IpN neurons after conditioning, paragraph 2; Figure 7-figure supplement 1. Data: dataset.

Criterion (claims file): US responses as in the Methods, on each cell's US-only trials; the "last 50 ms of the CS-US interval" reference has no CS here, so the readings are the 50 ms before the US (a) or the baseline alone (b). The paper does not say over which cells or from which reference the amplitudes (94.6 and 27.8 Hz) are taken; readings (i) all 25 cells, (ii) the cells showing each peak, each relative to baseline or to the 50 ms before the US. Reproduced when the counts are within tolerance and the amplitude test gives p < 0.05 with the second peak larger, under one reading.

Counts, over the 55 claims of the paper: 21 reproduced, 21 partially reproduced, 6 not reproduced, 7 blocked. Four of them use recording depth from Source data 1 (with_inputs): firing-rate-depth, fig4s1-cs-peak-suppression-not-different and fig6g-us-response-depth are reproduced and fig5ej-cs-pause-cells-shallower is blocked. The link claim source-data-1-link is reproduced. After the first verification round, seven outcomes changed: fig1ijk-modulation-classes and modulation-absolute-not-rate-dependent to not reproduced (no reading meets the criterion), fig1m, fig1no, us-pause-declines-with-training and fig6h-us-pause-trial-correlations to partially reproduced (the tests hold, some expected values do not), and fig7b-first-second-peak-correlated to partially reproduced (the correlation holds, the values do not). The second round agreed with all 56 outcomes; no change of outcome is proposed.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The paper links no analysis code, and several of its definitions are open (claims file, opening comment); every named reading is run, plus this attempt's variants (a+) of the baseline correction, a rebound span of 50 ms for the CS transients and the 0-212 ms window in the second dataset. Of these, only the 50 ms rebound decides an outcome: cs-pause-cells-have-us-pause meets its expected count of 6 +/- 1 only with it, and under the same span fig4b's association fails (2 of the 6 cells facilitate, Fisher p = 0.62 to 1), so those 6 cells do not behave like the paper's CS pause group. Under the claims file's readings that claim's Fisher test holds with 4 and 3 cells. The classification of cells does not reproduce the paper's counts under any reading (80 or 88 facilitation cells under the claims file's readings, against 60); the authors' own per-cell facilitation in Source data 1 follows reading (b) closely (Pearson r = 0.998, median difference -0.16 Hz) and gives 84 cells at 5 Hz, where reading (b) gives 88, so the paper's 60 rest on a criterion it does not state, and many downstream counts differ with it. The trial exclusions of the Methods are not applied again, since Source data 1 lists exactly the deposited trials as each cell's valid trials. This attempt's CR rule gives 111 recordings with behavior where Source data 1's CR flags give the paper's 103. The cross-correlation lags use the standard cross-covariance of the two traces, which puts at most one lag at the edge of the +/-100 ms range (one cell under class b in fig2l); the re-cut Pearson variant, used in the first round, put up to 26 cells there. Both give the same outcomes. The CS transient claims are each judged under any reading, and no single reading meets all eight of their criteria (the drop/mean reading meets five). The spike rate velocity is the first difference of the deposited 1 ms spike density, which gives values well above the paper's (for example 9.97 against 4.9 Hz/ms).

What was found about the data set. The file matches its published MD5. Recording depth, used by four claims, is not in the data set. The paper's Source data 1 on eLife gives it for the 270 first-dataset cells, which match the data set's cells by order on trial counts, per-trial eyelid closure at US onset and per-trial baseline rate, and gives none for the 102 second-dataset cells. The per-trial crAmplitude equals the eyelid position 13 ms before the stated US onset (exactly in the second dataset; in the first, the median per-recording largest difference is 1.1% closure), not at US onset as described. The per-trial facilitation follows reading (b) exactly in the second dataset over the whole 0-212 ms CS-US interval, not the last 200 ms, and only approximately in the first. The stored ephysMean is not the mean of the stored ephys trials in 26 recordings. 282 deposited trials have a baseline eyelid at or past half closure, which the Methods say were removed, although Source data 1 lists them among the valid trials. The first dataset has 18 mice, where the Results say 19 and the Methods 22. The US-only trials of 25 second-dataset cells and the optogenetic sessions are not deposited.
